Other QB updates: Malik Willis is still on IR for Miami with a groin injury that has now spread to his abdomen. Kyle McCord could be under centre against the Jets. In Baltimore, Lamar Jackson is still out with a thumb injury, and Jacoby Brissett is set to start against Houston. Elsewhere, Joe Milton will get another start for Philadelphia against Dallas, and Pittsburgh has opted to bench their healthy Aaron Rodgers in favor of Mason Rudolph for their Friday game against Denver.

ADVERTISEMENT

Running Backs

Several backfields are going to be significantly impacted in terms of workload going into Week 12, particularly given the relatively short Thanksgiving schedule.

ADVERTISEMENT

Kenneth Walker III (Chiefs, groin): Walker missed the Chiefs’ last two games with a groin injury. The Super Bowl MVP began a limited-basis practice on Tuesday following his absence on Monday. He is now working his way back to full participation to play Thursday night against the Bills. If he sits again, then Emmett Johnson will be the primary back.

Josh Jacobs (Packers, finger): Jacobs got a QD for Wednesday night’s game vs. the Rams. He’s been limited in practices with his finger. Fantasy managers will have to check his pregame status prior to Wednesday’s kickoff in Inglewood.

ADVERTISEMENT

Saquon Barkley (Eagles, neck/injury) and Kyren Williams (Rams, toe): Both players ready to go. Barkley left Sunday’s win over the Steelers in the 4th quarter with a neck sting. He was limited on the Monday estimate but upgraded to full participation on the Tuesday walkthrough report ahead of the Dallas game. Williams also moved up to full participation on the Monday estimate after a limited Sunday session and has no injury designation against Green Bay.

Other RB updates: In Indy, Seth McGowan is out for a while after a hamstring injury on a kick return in Week 11, so DJ Giddens will be the primary change-of-pace guy behind Jonathan Taylor.

ADVERTISEMENT

In Jacksonville, Bhayshul Tuten aggravated an ankle/foot injury in Week 11 but is could play through it and will share the snaps with Chris Rodriguez. Denver has designated Tyler Badie to return from IR with a thumb injury after he had a full practice, and Roschon Johnson in Chicago could be out for the week, having missed Monday’s walkthrough with an ankle injury.

Wide Receivers

Soft tissue injuries and the continuing setbacks have had a continuing effect on the wide receiver depth charts in both conferences.

ADVERTISEMENT

A.J. Brown (Patriots, hamstring): A.J. Brown’s return lasted one game. After missing Weeks 8–9 with ankle and knee issues, he came back against Detroit in Week 10 only to suffer a hamstring injury that will sideline him for weeks. He’s expected to be out for multiple weeks. This leaves the Patriots’ passing attack very thin with only backup QB Tommy DeVito available. The receiver group of DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, and Kyle Williams provides no reliable weekly fantasy floor.

Marvin Harrison Jr. (Texans, hamstring): Harrison could be out again for another game following a hamstring strain sustained in practice last week (Week 10). Head coach DeMeco Ryans called it a “short-term” injury. With Harrison out, Kayshon Boutte and Xavier Hutchinson will see a small increase in targets against Baltimore.

DeVonta Smith (Eagles, hamstring) and Rashee Rice (Chiefs, knee): Smith and Rice have practiced in full early in the week. Smith was in full participation in the Eagles’ Monday and Tuesday walkthroughs prior to their Thursday NFC East game in Dallas. Rice likewise practiced in full on both Monday and Tuesday for the Chiefs prior to heading to Buffalo.

ADVERTISEMENT

Other WR updates: Jets rookie Omar Cooper is questionable for Week 12 following an aggravated ankle injury in Week 10 and missing Week 11. With slot option Isaiah Williams also possibly out with a rib injury, it’s going to be Garrett Wilson and Adonai Mitchell who get the bulk of the targets against Miami.

In Pittsburgh, head coach Mike McCarthy was confident on Monday that Michael Pittman Jr. is expected to return from IR to face Denver after a foot injury. In Carolina, Jalen Coker went into the concussion protocol after taking a helmet-to-helmet hit in Week 11, though the Week 12 game against Tampa Bay on Monday night gives him some extra recovery time, and he is expected to be cleared for the game. Green Bay has both Bo Melton (thigh) and Skyy Moore (ankle) listed as questionable for Wednesday night’s game, and Dallas held Jonathan Mingo (ankle) out of their Tuesday walkthrough.

Tight Ends

Tight end availability is a mixture of key holiday returns and longer-term absences.

ADVERTISEMENT

Dalton Kincaid (Bills, thumb/ankle): Kincaid sat out Buffalo’s Week 11 win over Miami with his thumb and ankle still being managed. He did return to practice in a limited capacity on both Monday and Tuesday prior to Thursday night’s game against KC. His level of participation in practice on Wednesday will be a key indicator, but he’s likely to be in the game if he’s active and will presumably be back in TE1 status straight away.

Jake Ferguson (Cowboys, knee/ankle) and Dallas Goedert (Eagles, shin): On the other side of Thursday’s afternoon game, Ferguson missed both Monday and Tuesday practices with knee and ankle issues, meaning his chances of playing at Thanksgiving were very much in question. Goedert was the opposite story, moving from a limited Monday practice to full participation on Tuesday and is therefore clear to play against Dallas.

Terrance Ferguson (Rams, ankle/hamstring): Head coach Sean McVay has confirmed that Ferguson will have season-ending ankle surgery. LA have officially ruled him out for Wednesday night’s game against Green Bay.

Defensive Standouts and Notable IR Updates

Several significant defensive upgrades and injured reserve moves also impact the Week 12 picture.

ADVERTISEMENT

Micah Parsons (Packers, knee): Green Bay activated Parsons off the Reserve/Physically Unable to Perform list on Tuesday, following medical clearance after ACL surgery. He is officially listed as questionable after limited practice participation Sunday and Monday but is expected to make his 2026 season debut Wednesday. However, he is expected to make his 2026 season debut Wednesday night vs. the Rams.

Quinyon Mitchell (Eagles, hamstring) and Alex Highsmith (Steelers, ankle): Mitchell left Week 11 with a hamstring injury, missed the Monday walkthrough, and then returned as a very limited participant on Tuesday. Fangio is optimistic that Mitchell will be able to go against Dallas. In Pittsburgh, Highsmith didn’t practice on Tuesday while wearing an ankle brace, and McCarthy said it will be a real challenge for him to get on the field in a short week against Denver.

Players out for the season and on IR: Several notable contributors remain sidelined long-term or for the rest of the 2026 campaign:

QBS: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley and Malik Willis.

Running backs: De’Von Achane, TreVeyon Henderson, Tyjae Spears, RJ Harvey and Jawhar Jordan.

Wide receivers: Wan’Dale Robinson, Alec Pierce, Romeo Doubs, Jaylin Noel and Jayden Higgins.

Tight ends: Erick All, Durham Smythe and Terrance Ferguson.

Fullbacks: Ben VanSumeren (placed on IR by KC this week with a knee sprain).

What to Watch Before Week 12 Kickoff

Wednesday night’s Packers-Rams clash kicks off Week 12 with Micah Parsons set to debut and Josh Jacobs carrying a questionable tag. On Thanksgiving Day, final reports from practices will reveal whether Dalton Kincaid, Kenneth Walker III, Quinyon Mitchell, and Jake Ferguson can take the field. With a festive Sunday slate, Justin Herbert’s progress through the concussion protocol and Marvin Harrison Jr.’s hamstring recovery are critical checkpoints.

Final practice reports Wednesday and Thursday morning will settle the Thanksgiving slate. Fans need to monitor Kincaid, Walker, and Herbert’s status updates before locking in their lineups ahead of the kickoffs.

title: Green Bay's Week 12 injury report exposes the NFL's scheduling blunder
description:
Most of the time, teams get a full week of rest and preparation during their bye week, but the Green Bay Packers weren't afforded that same opportunity this year, despite needing it more than most.
Giving them a Week 11 bye is another.
But having those two things coincide is a slap in the face from the league's schedule-makers, who backed Green Bay into a corner at a time when they cannot afford it.
The Green Bay Packers' Week 12 injury report for Wednesday vs. the Rams is a direct result of the NFL's schedule oversight.
So the good news for Green Bay is that at least Los Angeles is in the same boat, with a Week 11 bye of their own.
text:
Most of the time, teams get a full week of rest and preparation during their bye week, but the Green Bay Packers weren't afforded that same opportunity this year, despite needing it more than most.

Green Bay entered a Week 11 bye knowing very well that they had a game on the Wednesday night before Thanksgiving on the horizon, and had to practice far earlier than any team normally would during its bye week. That was a problem in and of itself because the Packers have been banged up throughout the roster and needed the extra couple of days to set themselves right.

The situation is far more dire now that we have their injury report for Week 12, which is chock full of Questionable tags for key players. Those listed as questionable include Micah Parsons, who's supposed to make his long-awaited return, offensive linemen Sean Rhyan and Kevin Zeitler, linebacker Zaire Franklin, starting running back Josh Jacobs, and several others at key positions.

Giving the Packers a Wednesday night game is one thing. Giving them a Week 11 bye is another. But having those two things coincide is a slap in the face from the league's schedule-makers, who backed Green Bay into a corner at a time when they cannot afford it.

The Green Bay Packers' Week 12 injury report for Wednesday vs. the Rams is a direct result of the NFL's schedule oversight.

If you were wondering how many teams played on Thursday night coming out of a bye this season, the answer is zero. There are two teams playing on Wednesday night coming out of a bye, and those are the Packers and Rams. So the good news for Green Bay is that at least Los Angeles is in the same boat, with a Week 11 bye of their own.

But by that measure, these teams are both at a disadvantage like no other team in the entire NFL has faced this season. The difference between the Packers and Rams, however, is that Green Bay is stuck at the bottom of their division, fighting for their lives to make the postseason at all. And even in an off year, the Rams are one of the most fearsome opponents in the entire sport.

It's understandable to feature two of your marquee franchises in primetime during the week of Thanksgiving. From a popularity standpoint, it makes perfect sense. People will be near TVs at family homes, bars, and travel centers throughout the nation in the lead-up to Thanksgiving. But putting these teams at a legitimate disadvantage is a mistake that simply cannot stand.

If unusual injuries occur in this game, the NFL only has itself to blame. Fans of both teams will let it be known if that winds up being the case. However, some of the Packers' top players have a substantial chance of being ruled out because of this, and that's a blatant oversight by the league itself.

title: Micah Parsons' long-awaited return is here, so what should the Packers expect? - NFL.com
description:
Green Bay Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon recently joked he had never seen Parsons like that.
"Last year I just had all this energy," Parsons said Monday.
While Gannon has been game planning for Parsons' return since February, Parsons didn't inject himself into those preparations.
Will adding Parsons turn the Packers from good to great, like how they were with him on the field last season?
The Packers rank 15th in pressure percentage and 11th in sack rate without Parsons on the edge, according to TruMedia.
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- Micah Parsons' teammates have been teasing him lately.

He's been calm. Almost too calm.

Green Bay Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon recently joked he had never seen Parsons like that.

"Last year I just had all this energy," Parsons said Monday.

Don't mistake Parsons' lack of energy for fatigue, or his calm for indifference -- and he certainly isn't talking about slowing down on the field. Nixon even said Parsons seemed timid, according to No. 1 himself. Don't confuse that for worry, either.

If anything, Parsons is a lion -- the moniker he adopted as a rookie -- waiting to pounce.

And he's about to show his teeth.

Three hundred forty-seven days.

Fourteen games.

Countless days and nights, hard days and nights, wondering when his time would come.

On Wednesday night, under the bright lights of primetime in Los Angeles, the Packers' best player and one of the NFL's elites returns against the Rams in a virtual must-win game for both 6-4 teams.

"It's built up," Parsons said of his energy. "They like, 'Are you nervous?' No, I'm just so focused. I'm so locked in on what's ahead of me, and I understand what this game Wednesday means to the organization and myself and what it means for playoffs."

The Packers were 9-3-1 at the time of Parsons' injury last season. They held first place in the NFC North and the No. 2 seed in the NFC. When Parsons crumbled to the ground Dec. 14 while chasing Broncos quarterback Bo Nix, the Packers were winning that game, too, against the AFC's eventual No. 1 seed. As Parsons collapsed, so too did his team.

Without its finisher -- a player former defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley compared to legendary New York Yankees closer Mariano Rivera -- Green Bay blew two-score leads against the Broncos, the following week in Chicago and then again at Soldier Field in the playoffs. Without its best player, the team's season ended on a five-game losing streak.

Parsons tore his ACL and meniscus that day nearly a year ago in Denver. To an outsider, his return has taken too long. Some inside 1265 Lombardi Ave., and even Parsons himself, might agree, at least compared to initial expectations.

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes tore his ACL the same day and returned in plenty of time for Week 1. Parsons will be making his debut in Week 12.

It's important to understand the severity of Parsons' injury and how that lengthened his rehab. In addition to undergoing left ACL surgery 15 days after the initial injury (once swelling subsided), he underwent a full lateral and medial meniscus repair.

While some walk three weeks after surgery, Parsons' quad was still "fully dead" at that point. He didn't get off crutches until about two months after the procedure.

"Everyone's timelines are different," Parsons said earlier this month after returning to practice. "I had a lot of damage done to my leg, and I think it's a miracle that I'm even standing here today."

Over the past three weeks, Parsons has progressed from individual drills to limited action in 11-on-11 work. Tight end Tucker Kraft recently said Parsons bull-rushed him in practice and has looked great. Coach Matt LaFleur and quarterback Jordan Love agreed.

Parsons said he has received great feedback from teammates and feels "really, really confident" in his body entering his return.

Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon was recently asked how often since taking the Packers job he has game-planned for when Parsons comes back.

"Every day," he said.

So what exactly should we expect when Parsons steps on the field Wednesday night at SoFi Stadium -- a venue he hopes to revisit in February for Super Bowl LXI?

For starters, Parsons will almost certainly be on a snap count. Whether he stays within that snap count is a different story. He cautioned not to expect his normal 50 to 60 plays, though he stopped short of saying he'll obey a strict limit.

"Nah, I think once I'm in the zone, I'm in the zone and people don't really mess with you when you're in a zone," Parsons said. "At this point, we can say every game is gonna be the difference between playoffs or Cancún."

Parsons also said not to expect a consistently All-Pro-caliber player until later in the season. He warned that he'll put some "terrible" plays on film as he establishes his footing in game action, but added there will be flashes of the Parsons who has earned four All-Pro honors and five Pro Bowl nods in his first five seasons.

"I know what type of player I am, and I know what type of player I'm gonna be when I come back," he said.

While Gannon has been game planning for Parsons' return since February, Parsons didn't inject himself into those preparations. He said Monday that before asking anything of his new play caller, he wanted to first prove to Gannon what he could do on the field after so much time away.

His teammates have already taken notice. Rookie edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton, a fellow Penn State product, recently watched Parsons practive and asked the veteran if he was always that fast.

"It's just the intent of how we should practice and how we should go about things and how we should be preparing," Parsons told him. "He's learning, and I'm showing coach how good I can move and how I feel and now he's like, 'Man, you feel really confident.' … However they want to incorporate and add to the system, I just got to be open and ready and willing to learn."

The Packers are currently sitting in the same No. 7 seed they've entered the playoffs with in 2023, 2024 and 2025. They've shown flashes of brilliance and spurts of mind-numbing incompetence. Will adding Parsons turn the Packers from good to great, like how they were with him on the field last season? Maybe, but their pass rush hasn't exactly been a problem.

The Packers rank 15th in pressure percentage and 11th in sack rate without Parsons on the edge, according to TruMedia. The likes of Brenton Cox Jr., Dennis-Sutton and Karl Brooks have exceeded expectations along the defensive line. Maybe it would help more if Parsons played offensive line, but nobody inside the building is complaining about adding an elite player to an already stout defense.

Even if Parsons is only his typical self in small increments until later in the year, they'll take it.

"He's one of the best players in the National Football League," wide receiver Christian Watson said. "So to get him back out there, just his presence out there will be big time for us. Obviously just the energy that he'll bring just with his play style and even his energy on the sideline will be huge, so definitely excited for him to be back out there."

When Parsons steps between the white lines Wednesday night, his family and friends will be in the stands. Parsons bluntly said he doesn't care for their support as much as they'd like, viewing friends and family as distractions when he just wants to play.

Maybe that shows just how locked in Parsons is. And when a player of his caliber sets his sights on something, good luck stopping him.

"I've achieved everything that I've wanted in my career except for the big one," Parsons said, referring to the Super Bowl. "That's kind of like my own mindset, and through the (Nick) Saban documentary, I learned just stay in the process of every day. Own my process today, so I owned it today. I got another process tomorrow. And God willing, I'll have another process Wednesday night, and that'll be the start of this new journey."

title: Agent's Take: The Puka Nacua predicament and where his future with Rams stands after injury
description:

The last wide receiver to be dealt after receiving a franchise tag is Adams in 2022.
Hill replaced Adams as the NFL's highest-paid wide receiver on a severely backloaded four-year contract extension as a part of the trade.
This could mean fewer contract guarantees than in the top wide receiver deals and significant per-game active roster bonuses.
The largest per-game roster bonus currently in a wide receiver contract is Christian Watson's with the Packers.
text:
Puka Nacua has nobody to blame but himself for a $5.77 million salary this year while playing out his four-year rookie contract. Based strictly on production, the 2023 fifth-round pick should have already become the NFL's highest-paid wide receiver ahead of Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who received a four-year contract extension averaging $42.15 million per year with a wide receiver record $120.1 million in overall guarantees in March. Instead, Nacua created his own problems.

Nacua started his career like gangbusters. He set single-season rookie records with 105 receptions and 1,486 receiving yards in 2023. The receptions record has since been broken, but the receiving yards mark still stands.

Nacua led the NFL with 129 receptions for 1,715 yards and 10 touchdowns, all career highs, last season. The 129 receptions are tied as the seventh-best single-season total in league history, and Nacua's 107.2 receiving yards per game led the NFL last year. He also carried the ball 10 times for 105 yards with a touchdown.

However, the Los Angeles Rams weren't comfortable giving the two-time All-Pro a massive payday during the offseason because of off-the-field issues. Nacua tried to sneak live streamers into the Rams practice facility against head coach Sean McVay's wishes late last season. During the livestream, Nacua performed a suggested touchdown dance with a gesture considered antisemitic, for which he apologized. More concerning, a lawsuit was filed against Nacua in March alleging he bit a woman while intoxicated and made antisemitic statements on New Year's Eve. Nacua spent time during the offseason in a holistic care facility to focus on personal growth and overall behavioral improvement.

The 2026 season hasn't gone how the Rams and Nacua expected. The Rams were heavy preseason favorites to win Super Bowl LXI before the season started. A 6-4 record after 10 games didn't seem imaginable. But that's the case. Making the playoffs won't be easy, and the Rams have the NFL's hardest remaining schedule.

Nacua chances at a Rams payday are gone

A performance comparable to 2025's, when Nacua was an NFL Offensive Player of the Year finalist, while putting his troubles behind him would have provided ammunition to push for becoming the NFL's highest-paid non-quarterback, as fellow wide receivers Justin Jefferson and Ja'Marr Chase did in 2024 and 2025 on their respective deals with the Minnesota Vikings and Cincinnati Bengals. But that distinction currently belongs to Houston Texans edge rusher Will Anderson Jr., who signed a three-year, $150 million extension averaging $50 million per year (with $134.1 million of guarantees).

Anderson-type money is no longer a possibility. Nacua's fortunes took a turn for the worse when he suffered a sprained MCL, sprained PCL and turf toe in his right leg at the end of Week 9's win over the Washington Commanders. Nacua wasn't initially put on injured reserve, which requires a four-game absence, because the hope was he would miss about a month of action. A hip/groin problem also kept Nacua out of the Week 2 and Week 3 games.

The off-the-field transgressions took center stage again last week when the NFL suspended Nacua three games for violating the personal conduct policy. In a controversial but not unprecedented move, Nacua is being allowed to serve his suspension while on IR. Since Nacua was already going to miss these games, the suspension is essentially just a fine of three weeks' salary costing Nacua $961,167.

It was later revealed that Nacua is out for the season after having surgery to repair his torn MCL last Tuesday. The NFL reportedly was unaware that Nacua had undergone surgery when imposing the suspension two days later.

Nacua's future in LA remains uncertain

Nacua now finishes the 2026 season with 70 catches for 715 yards with four touchdowns in seven games. He was tied for the NFL's third-most receptions and ranked seventh in receiving yards following Week 9. Nacua's 102.1 receiving yards per game are second in the league.

The expected four- to five-month recovery time means Nacua won't be healthy before free agency begins on March 11. Speculation that Nacua has played his final game for the Rams is premature, but McVay gave mixed messages about Nacua on Monday. He stressed Nacua's importance to the team but couldn't guarantee his return next season.

It's unlikely the Rams are going to let Nacua walk out the door via the open market. The Rams would only get a 2028 third-round compensatory draft pick at best for Nacua signing with another team in free agency.

Nacua appears to be destined for a franchise tag in the offseason before the 15-day designation period expires March 3. Under the NFL collective bargaining agreement's formula for non-exclusive franchise tags, the 2027 wide receiver number is projected to be 8.86% of the 2027 salary cap. That's down from this year's 9.063%.

That means the 2027 wide receiver franchise tag should be $28.661 million, with next year's salary cap being set at $323.5 million. A 7.4% increase in the salary cap over the current $301.2 million figure would be consistent with the 7.88% growth from 2025.

The non-exclusive tag allows a player to negotiate with other NFL teams. If an offer sheet is signed with another club, the player's team has five days to match the offer. Two first-round picks are the compensation from the signing team if the offer sheet is not matched.

An exclusive franchise tag, typically reserved for quarterbacks, is impractical due to cost. There's a different calculation in this situation: The average of the top five 2027 wide receiver salaries (salary cap numbers with some minor adjustments) at the end of the restricted free agent signing period (April 23). Initially, the non-exclusive number is used as a placeholder and adjusted upwards if the exclusive calculation dictates once restricted free agency ends.

The 2027 exclusive wide receiver franchise tag currently projects to $42.247 million. Smith-Njigba's wide receiver market-setting average yearly salary is slightly below the projected tag. This number is subject to change depending on new wide receiver deals, contract restructures, pay cuts and/or releases between now and then.

An offer sheet is prohibited with the exclusive designation. A player under an exclusive franchise tag cannot negotiate with other teams. It is a "closed" negotiation.

LA's options for Nacua

Franchise tag: Accommodating the non-exclusive franchise tag shouldn't be an issue. The Rams have the NFL's fifth-fewest 2027 salary cap commitments at $236.997 million with 37 players under contract and a little less than $3.83 million in existing 2026 cap space that can be carried over, according to NFLPA data. The league average is $298.84 million, with 41 players under contract (rounded to the nearest whole number).

Sign a long-term deal: Nacua surely doesn't want to play under a franchise tag in 2027 after missing out on an opportunity to cash in this year and having another injury-plagued season. The Rams and Nacua would have until July 15 to sign a long-term deal per CBA rules. Nacua's career earnings from his rookie contract are just under $7.75 million. He also missed five games in 2024 because of a PCL sprain in his right knee, so Nacua has only played 51 games in his four NFL seasons. Playing with reckless abandon seems to make Nacua more susceptible to injury than most other wide receivers.

Nacua receives an offer sheet from another team: Nacua is the type of talent a team would seriously consider signing to an offer sheet under ordinary circumstances. No wide receiver has ever been more productive than Nacua through his first 51 NFL games. Nacua's 383 receptions are the most ever during that span and 28 more than second place. His 4,906 receiving yards are bettered only by Jefferson's 4,975. Nacua's 96.2 receiving yards per game are the most in NFL history.

However, Durability concerns and Nacua's baggage could limit offer sheet interest even though high-impact non-quarterbacks are being traded for more than two first-round picks.

The Chicago Bears acquired All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick from the Tennessee Titans for a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fourth-round pick at the end of October. The New York Jets dealt All-Pro cornerback Sauce Gardner to the Indianapolis Colts for a 2026 first-round pick (16th overall), a 2027 first-round pick and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell at last year's trade deadline.

Rams need to restock draft picks after tough 2026 season

Getting draft capital while avoiding a massive investment in Nacua may make sense for the Rams after a Super Bowl-or-bust season. After all, the 2026 and 2027 first-round picks and more were sacrificed to bring in cornerback Trent McDuffie and edge rusher Myles Garrett, the reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year. A bust seems more likely since the Rams wouldn't make the playoffs if the season ended today.

The Rams could be facing a transition year in 2027 anyway, as there could be major roster turnover. A conscious decision was made to let a stellar 2023 draft class, which includes offensive guard Steve Avila, offensive tackle Warren McClendon Jr., defensive tackle Kobie Turner, and edge rusher Byron Young, in addition to Nacua, play out their rookie contracts. Plus, future first-ballot Hall of Famer Aaron Donald ended his two-year retirement in August to return for a Super Bowl run on a one-year, $20 million deal (worth a maximum of $30 million through incentives).

Other key Rams, such as wide receiver Davante Adams, offensive guard Kevin Dotson, tight end Colby Parkinson and center Coleman Shelton, will also be unrestricted free agents. Quarterback Matthew Stafford, the reigning NFL MVP, is showing his age (38) and could retire, although he signed a one-year extension for $55 million in May.

Is an offseason trade possible?

A sign-and-trade would be more likely than an offer sheet if the Rams and/or Nacua want a fresh start. The last wide receiver to be dealt after receiving a franchise tag is Adams in 2022. The Green Bay Packers got a 2022 first-round pick (22nd overall) and a 2022 second-round pick from the Las Vegas Raiders. Adams became the league's highest-paid wide receiver on an extremely backloaded five-year deal.

A franchise player hasn't moved for the unmatched offer sheet compensation in over 25 years. Wide receiver Joey Galloway, who received the exclusive designation, went from the Seahawks to the Dallas Cowboys in 2000 for a 2000 first-round pick (19th overall) and a 2001 first-round pick (seventh overall). Galloway signed a deal making him the NFL's then-second-highest-paid wide receiver in connection with the trade.

Shortly after Adams was dealt, the Miami Dolphins acquired Tyreek Hill from the Kansas City Chiefs for five draft picks: 2022 first (29th overall), second and fourth round picks, as well as 2023 fourth and sixth round picks. Hill replaced Adams as the NFL's highest-paid wide receiver on a severely backloaded four-year contract extension as a part of the trade. Hill had engaged in more egregious conduct than Nacua. He was almost three years removed from any allegations when the Dolphins paid him.

There's a common denominator in each of these cases. A team was willing to give up significant draft capital and pay top dollar to the wide receivers.

Nacua could still be in line for sizeable raise, with conditions

Whether Nacua remains with the Rams long-term, leaves on an unmatched offer sheet or goes through a sign-and-trade, resetting the wide receiver market isn't out of the question. That's despite missing a season's worth of games over his four NFL seasons and having non-football issues.

Odell Beckham Jr. also missed 17 games in his first four years, like Nacua. A broken left ankle cost Beckham the final 12 games of the 2017 season. The injuries didn't prevent the New York Giants from putting Beckham at the top of the receiver pay scale with a five-year contract extension.

Nacua switched his representation to Win Sports Group in August, so he shares agents with Smith-Njigba. It wouldn't be surprising for Nacua's camp to seek a deal averaging at least $45 million per year, with as much as $125 million in overall guarantees plus somewhere near $95 million fully guaranteed at signing. Both guarantee marks would be new standards for wide receivers.

The team that pays Nacua would be wise to insist on a team-friendly structure. This could mean fewer contract guarantees than in the top wide receiver deals and significant per-game active roster bonuses. The primary benefit of the roster bonuses is that they provide a team with some financial relief with injuries. The per-game amount is only payable if the player is on the active roster for that particular game.

The largest per-game roster bonus currently in a wide receiver contract is Christian Watson's with the Packers. Watson has $2.125 million annually ($125,000 for each game active) from 2027 through 2030.

A team making a huge financial commitment with Nacua would be betting that he isn't a buyer beware proposition. The return on investment would be poor if Nacua's problems aren't behind him or injuries continued to mount with his physical style of play.

Joel Corry is a former sports agent who helped found Premier Sports & Entertainment, a sports management firm that represents professional athletes and coaches. Prior to his tenure at Premier, Joel worked for Management Plus Enterprises, which represented Shaquille O'Neal, Hakeem Olajuwon and Ronnie Lott.

text:
Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III will miss his third game in a row with a groin injury, as Kansas City has already ruled him out for Thursday's Thanksgiving matchup against the Buffalo Bills, per NFL Network.

Walker's 872 rushing yards and seven rushing touchdowns lead the Chiefs in his first season with the team after spending four years with the Seattle Seahawks, but he hasn't played since a 35-12 win over the New York Jets in Week 9 thanks to a groin injury suffered at practice before Kansas City's Week 10 matchup against the Atlanta Falcons.

Starting in place of Walker once again is rookie Emmett Johnson, who also started for the veteran running back in the previous two games. Johnson is second on the Chiefs with 317 rushing yards and two touchdowns on the ground, with 101 and 105 rushing yards in the previous two games. He's averaging 4.5 yards per carry, behind Walker's NFL-leading 5.5 yards per but nearly half-a-yard ahead of the league average mark in 2026.

The fifth-round pick out of Nebraska was averaging 3.3 carries per game before Walker's injury, and has logged 22 and 23 in his two starts.

Last week, coach Andy Reid said that the injury was just "a day-to-day thing," and that the team was being cautious while it could afford to. "It's getting better, but with those (injuries), you don't want to do something stupid, put him out there." The Bills are a significant challenge and step up from the Falcons and Arizona Cardinals, last week's opponent for Kansas City, but Buffalo also isn't the last hurdle for the Chiefs, either.

After 9-1 Buffalo on the road, the Chiefs face the 6-4 Rams — winners of four in a row after a rough start — in Los Angeles next Thursday. Then it's on to Cincinnati and the first-place, 7-1 Bengals to end the three-game road trip, before hosting the New England Patriots and San Francisco 49ers at home.

Essentially, Reid's stance from last week remains: the Chiefs want Walker back right, not just back, rather than risking an extended period without him around when Kansas City needs him most.

Kenneth Walker III will sit out his third straight game this Thursday when the Chiefs play on Thanksgiving in Buffalo, the team announced Wednesday.

Walker has been sidelined for the Chiefs' last two games with a groin injury. He rejoined practice Tuesday for the first time since suffering his injury but was listed as "limited."

It has been 13 days since Walker suffered his injury during a Nov. 12 practice.

Chadiha noted Walker's return might have been impacted by the Chiefs' quick turnaround between last Sunday's win over the Arizona Cardinals and Thursday's holiday matchup. The Thursday game could also be impacted by rain.

Buffalo is also coming off the first three-game stretch without a touchdown allowed over a 43-drive scoreless stretch that marks the NFL's longest since 2019, although that run took place against three injury-limited opponents in the Minnesota Vikings, New York Jets and Miami Dolphins.

Johnson could continue making his case for a bigger role in the Chiefs' lineup if he is able to help his team snap that streak Thursday.

After the Bills, the Chiefs are slated face the most effective run defense in the league in a Dec. 3 Thursday matchup against the Los Angeles Rams.

The Rams have allowed an NFL-low 96.8 yards on the ground per game so far this season. Kansas City could be hoping letting Walker recover for another week will increase the likelihood he is able to return before that Week 13 matchup.

text:
IT WAS LATE in the fourth quarter against the Washington Commanders and coach Sean McVay and the Los Angeles Rams needed a first down to win the game.

Facing a third-and-11 with 1 minute, 44 seconds to go, McVay called a jet sweep to Rams star wide receiver Puka Nacua, the player he and quarterback Matthew Stafford often turn to with the game on the line. Nacua was tackled after a 5-yard gain. He stayed down longer than usual after the hit, but eventually walked off the field.

The Rams won that Week 9 game to improve to 5-4, but the hit to Nacua was costly. The tackle left the fourth-year wideout with a sprained MCL and PCL in his right knee, as well as turf toe. Nacua had surgery on his MCL a week ago, and his recovery time is expected to be four to five months, forcing him to miss the rest of this season, including the playoffs. He is expected to be ready for the start of the 2027 season.

The day after the surgery, the NFL announced that Nacua was suspended for three games for violating the league's personal conduct policy. The suspension came after a woman in Los Angeles filed a lawsuit in March alleging Nacua made an "unprovoked antisemitic statement" and later bit her on the shoulder. Nacua denied the allegations and later entered a rehab center.

Nacua is in the final season of his rookie deal, one the 2023 fifth-round pick has outplayed since his historic rookie year. But will he actually be back in Los Angeles next season? While the Rams have acknowledged both his off-the-field incidents and the way his physical play style affects his availability, neither changes the Rams' thinking about a contract extension, a team source said.

"I think you're watching young guys -- no different than I'm continuing to try to mature as a man -- figure out how do you navigate these responsibilities in all parts of your life being a professional," McVay said this week. "And I think he's growing and I trust his heart and I think he's making a lot of steps that are in the right direction.

"I'm bummed for him that he got injured. It was a tough year because he kind of was banged up and playing through stuff, even more so than normal just with the style of play. And then obviously his season is over now with regards to him getting that surgery, but do expect him to return and be back in a couple months and ready to go."

When asked whether he expects Nacua to be a key player in 2027, McVay said while the Rams have a long list of pending free agents, Nacua is "a huge part of the conversation."

"He's obviously a guy that is a very important piece for us for now and for the future, but there's a lot of guys that fall into that category," McVay said.

There's no doubt Nacua is a difference-maker for this Rams offense. The wide receiver has a 26% target share in his career, the sixth highest among anyone with at least 50 games played since 2023, per ESPN Research.

"I can't see him anywhere else than being here," Rams team captain Quentin Lake said. "He has been such a cornerstone of this franchise for the last four years, but at the same time, whatever happens, happens. And we're all hoping that everything gets figured out and that he does stay. I think that's everybody's main priority. And I'm always in his corner as well."

RAMS WIDE RECEIVERS coach Eric Yarber has a motto for his room: "You can't live forever, so don't try to."

No one embodies that more than Nacua, whose style of physical play is part of what makes him so good and has made him such an ideal fit in McVay's offense.

"[Nacua] talks about being the hammer, not the nail," Yarber told ESPN last season. "And that makes your run after catch that much more violent. DBs don't want to hit you; they're going to go low and they lose their technique and stuff like that. So when you're physical -- more physical than them -- they don't want to tackle you."

But with that physicality comes a cost: Nacua has not played a full season since his rookie campaign. After Nacua's season-ending hit in Washington in Week 9, McVay was asked about the playcall. The Rams were up by a touchdown and McVay and the Rams knew one more first down would effectively end the game. Instead, the Rams had to punt the ball back to Jayden Daniels and the Commanders. McVay said he'd be lying if he hadn't "questioned the decision-making on that last play over and over in my head."

"It's stuff that I feel tremendous responsibility for, and we have to be able to figure out how to protect these guys while also putting them in positions that help our team and allow them to be able to shine," McVay said. "He's a guy that we have to be intentional about because it's a bummer and because he can do so much, you want to make sure you don't take that for granted."

But while McVay said he and Nacua have talked about the possibility of not always taking big hits, "that's like telling a tiger not to be a tiger."

Nacua missed two games earlier this season after injuring his hip during practice. He missed just one game in 2025 with an ankle injury, but he was on injured reserve for five games the previous season with a knee injury.

"We try to educate them on situations," McVay said. "Where are the things that you can avoid? I do also believe ... part of that responsibility is on myself to make sure, how much are you exposing him to those types of plays? And it's not something that I take lightly."

During training camp, Nacua was asked for his personal goals entering the season.

"I think staying healthy is one of the biggest things," Nacua said. "I know that physicality that I play with I don't think it's ever going to change. It's ingrained in me, so continue to take care of my body in the ways that I need to."

IN MCVAY'S FIRST public comments after the lawsuit against Nacua came out in March of this year, the coach said the team had known about the incident since it happened on New Year's Eve and that he trusted Nacua and wanted to "be able to put my arm around him."

It was not Nacua's first off-the-field incident. In mid-December 2025, Nacua issued a statement to apologize for performing a gesture on an internet livestream that was "antisemitic in nature and perpetuated harmful stereotypes against Jewish people." On that same livestream, he said he thinks some NFL referees make calls just to get shown on TV during games.

Nacua released the statement the morning before the Rams played the Seattle Seahawks on Dec. 18. That night after the game, Nacua tweeted, "Can you say i was wrong. Appreciate you stripes for your contribution. Lol."

In the 2026 offseason, Nacua became eligible for a contract extension. Based on his on-field production, Nacua was expected to be in line for a record-setting payday. Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who was a first-round pick in Nacua's draft class, reset the market in March when he signed a four-year, $168.6 million contract extension that made him the highest-paid receiver in NFL history.

When McVay talked about the lawsuit involving Nacua at the NFL's annual meetings at the end of March, he acknowledged that while the receiver's "play on the field is amazing," there is also "a responsibility in terms of representing all things, not exclusive to just that."

"He knows that," McVay said at the time, "Those are the expectations and we're hopeful that that'll be something that this will be an opportunity for him to learn and grow. And we are hopeful that he's a Ram for a really long time, but he understands what the responsibility is, not exclusive to just the production on the field."

Nacua entered training camp without a contract extension. The 25-year-old said he didn't consider holding out in an effort to get the extension done. He also acknowledged that his off-the-field incidents affected a potential contract extension.

"I try to take accountability for the things that I know that I can continue to change," Nacua said. "I can grow in ways that have helped me feel as best as I can when I step out here on the football field and outside of the football field."

Nacua was suspended for three games by the NFL, which he is serving while on injured reserve. The suspension will effectively be a fine, as Nacua will lose $950,000 in game checks, according to ESPN's Field Yates.

The league also communicated to Nacua, a source told ESPN's Adam Schefter, that any further violation of the personal conduct policy, including failing to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program, will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the league.

During training camp, McVay said he didn't want to put a timeline on when a contract extension might take place, because "I don't think you want to dangle a carrot that way."

"I think he's inspired to do right because his heart is right," McVay said in July. "I think the contract and things like that will take care of itself because he's an incredible player. Like anything else, he's continuing to mature as a man. I love him. I love his heart and I love the growth that he's had and we're with him every step of the way."

McVay's tone had not changed in late November when asked about Nacua's future with the team. While he acknowledged the long list of pending free agents Los Angeles has, he said, "there are mechanics that we'd like to be able to try to figure out how to keep these really good players and people that we love."

ONE OF THOSE "mechanics" is the exclusive franchise tag, which Over the Cap currently estimates to be nearly $31 million in 2027. Should the Rams use that tag on Nacua, it would allow the sides until July 15 to agree to a long-term contract or instead act as a one-year contract for the star receiver.

The Rams have not used the franchise tag since 2018, when they used the non-exclusive franchise tag on safety Lamarcus Joyner.

Behind Nacua, the Rams don't have much depth under contract for the 2027 season. Veteran wide receiver Davante Adams, who has been on injured reserve since injuring his hamstring in Week 6, is a pending free agent. McVay has not said when Adams will return to practice, but said he thought it would be on the shorter end of the initial six-to-10-week timeline. Adams, 33, has not said how much longer he wants to play, but said last season that he already told Stafford that whenever the quarterback retires, he will retire, too.

Since Nacua was drafted three years ago, the Rams have run 2,519 plays with him on the field. On those plays, they are averaging six yards per play, a 41% conversion rate on third down and a Total QBR of 67. In their 1,379 plays without Nacua, they average 5.2 yards per play, a 37% conversion rate on third down and a Total QBR of 56.

Adams has the highest team target share on plays without Nacua on the field since 2023 (21%), according to ESPN Research. Adams is the only Rams player at 20% or higher.

Tight end Terrance Ferguson, a second-round pick in 2025, was expected to be an important part of this Rams offense this season. He played in just three games before an ankle injury forced him to be placed on injured reserve.

On Monday, McVay said the tight end needs season-ending ankle surgery. Rookie tight end Max Klare, a second-round pick, does not have a catch this season. Tight ends Colby Parkinson and Davis Allen are free agents, as well.

Lake, who was playing the final season of his rookie contract last season, signed a contract extension right after coming off injured reserve. While the safety said he and Nacua are in different situations because of the length of their injuries, he knows how much the receiver means to the organization.

"He's been one of the best receivers in the league for the last three years and there's no lying -- the film always tells the truth," Lake said. "So I know there's a lot of things. Injury sucks, dealing with suspension is tough too, but at the end of the day, I think we know and understand who he is as a person and as a player. But he'll be all right. I think you go through things that challenge you and you go through things that create the person and man that you're supposed to become."

There were already two changes by this point last season (Titans and Giants), but zero teams have moved on from their head coaches so far in 2026. What's the latest on hot seats around the league? Could we really make it through the regular season with no jobs coming open?

With Daniel Jones and Brandon Aiyuk both clearing waivers and becoming free agents this week, our insiders also asked around on potential landing spots for them. And while Puka Nacua's season might be over, his future is a big talker right now. Fowler and Graziano tried to get a sense of what comes next for the star receiver and whether the Rams will hand him a big extension in the offseason. And finally, they canvased the league for a quick poll of who should win MVP as of now.

It's all here, as Fowler and Graziano answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 12.

Jump to:

Head coach hot seat updates

Fits for Jones, Aiyuk | MVP candidates

Nacua's future | Fantasy advice

Still no coaching changes? Where do things stand for head coaches on the hot seat?

Graziano: Well, it's not like no team has done anything. The Colts fired their GM weeks ago. The Panthers fired their defensive coordinator. The Cardinals fired their defensive coordinator. The Cowboys didn't fire their defensive coordinator, instead demoted him and kept him around to suffer with everyone else. But you want to know about head coaches, so fine. Situations I'm watching for potential change at the end of the season include the Jets, Buccaneers, Colts, Eagles and maybe Commanders, though Dan Quinn seems to be turning things around in D.C.

Would any of those teams move on from their head coach before the end of the season? I personally doubt it, in large part because I'm not sure which coordinators or assistants would be candidates to have audition roles the rest of the season. It is still early, and things could get bad enough in one or more of these spots that a team could decide to change for change's sake, but that's my read right now. Jeremy, how did I do?

Fowler: Nailed it! To be fair, there's usually a coaching change by this part of the season. The Titans' Brian Callahan and the Giants' Brian Daboll were properly fired before this point last season. Thanksgiving spelled the end for Chicago's Matt Eberflus in 2024. In 2023, Carolina's Frank Reich and Las Vegas' Josh McDaniels were gone before December. So, change is inevitable, and possibly soon. But I'm with you for this season, Dan -- it seems several ownership groups are willing to show some level of patience with their hot-seat coaches.

That seems to be the case in Washington, where Quinn is rallying the Commanders and has a soft schedule coming up. The Bucs could wait until season's end for clarity on Todd Bowles' future, though Monday night vs. Carolina feels important (the Bucs would be three games out in the NFC South with a loss). It seems like Aaron Glenn, fresh off a win, should get the rest of the season with the Jets. Why not give him more time to see what he can do? There's no real rush there. So, if we're taking temperatures, your gauge on the five jobs above is correct, and I'll raise you a few more for the radar: the Saints and Cowboys.

Saints coach Kellen Moore making run-game staff changes during the bye week wasn't the best sign. And the vibes out of Dallas leadership are not great. The Christian Parker move was not universally well-received in the building. This might be a case where coach Brian Schottenheimer needs a playoff berth to ensure a third season.

Graziano: A wild note I saw recently is that the Saints have trailed in all 27 games in which Moore has been their head coach. They must figure out if Tyler Shough is their long-term future at QB, and if they don't think Moore is the coach to help get the most out of him, that could spell trouble, even after only two seasons.

And I agree on Schottenheimer. The Cowboys are more patient with coaches than their reputation would lead you to believe, but they had very high hopes for this season. If it fizzles out because they blew the defensive coordinator hire, and Schottenheimer gets to the end of the year with another losing record, I think there would be some smoke there.

Fowler: The Chargers are firmly on the radar despite coach Jim Harbaugh's massive buyout on a five-year deal (do the math on what was reported as a five-year, $80 million deal in 2024). If Harbaugh finishes, say, 2-15 in Los Angeles, ownership must do some soul searching at that point, no? (Particularly when the team plays home games in a stadium it doesn't even own.) And if the Chargers still believe in Harbaugh, the bigger question becomes: Do they trust him to hire a third offensive coordinator in as many years? The Mike McDaniel hire has been flashy but has produced a 30th-ranked scoring offense and lack of a clear identity. The McDaniel era pales in comparison to the Greg Roman era (Roman is thriving with the Giants, by the way).

And Tennessee seems like one to watch because of the Titans' penchant for firings in recent years. I'm curious whether Tennessee breaks precedent and gives Robert Saleh time. The roster is not good, but no rebuild is ever easy for the coach because of the inevitably bad product. The Titans are 1-9, and a 51-30 loss to Dallas prompted Saleh to call his defense "dogs---" in a news conference. I'm not sure where to go with that, but what I'm saying is Tennessee is usually a wild card based on recent history.

Daniel Jones and Brandon Aiyuk are suddenly free agents after their respective releases. What's next, and where they could land?

Fowler: Let's start with Jones. Now that he has cleared waivers, he must weigh whether to sign somewhere right away or wait this out to see what develops injury-wise around the league as the playoffs approach. Some people I've talked to inside the league wonder whether he'll choose the latter. The natural fit right now is New England, which is 5-5 and will be without Drake Maye for what looks like the rest of the regular season. But head coach Mike Vrabel seems intent on starting Tommy DeVito, at least this week. So, maybe that's the play -- wait this week out, see what happens with New England or if another team develops an opening.

But I'm not sure which job would actually rebuild Jones' free agency value at this point. It depends what's important to him: a chance to start, take over for an older quarterback, be next season's bridge guy or learn a new system on a winning team.

Graziano: If I were considering signing Jones, I'd be thinking more about next season than this one based on everything we've seen from him this year. An Achilles injury is awfully serious, and he wouldn't be the first player we've seen look a lot better in his second season after that surgery than his first. The notion that the 2026 version of Jones could step in and help save someone's season is farfetched.

I believe the Patriots want to go with DeVito in the hopes that he can keep their train on the track, but as we saw with that disastrous Carson Wentz start for the Vikings a couple of Monday nights ago, poor performance can absolutely change a team's plan. Jones seems like a guy who's going to get another chance somewhere at some point, but my expectations for him being a significant help to a team the rest of this season are quite low.

Fowler: As for Aiyuk, teams I've spoken to this week have real reservations about whether he gets a job right away, though those conversations occurred before news of his midweek visit to Washington. "I think he's unemployed for a bit," an NFC exec said. At least three unknown variables exist: health, conditioning and motivation. On the flip side, buying low isn't the worst thing. He's only 28, and practice squads are tailored for fliers like this. Is Washington a natural home for him, Dan, or is there a better option?

Graziano: Washington always seemed like the spot, and you reported that he and Jayden Daniels have mended fences since the summer. But rookie Antonio Williams is playing quite well for the Commanders, and my sense is they like what they're getting from Stefon Diggs and Treylon Burks. I'm not sure how desperate they are for help right now. I wonder if the Rams would look at him if they win Wednesday and still have a chance to make the run they expected to make. Arizona is desperate at that position, but I'm not sure he'd want to go there. New England could use help, too.

But to your initial point, teams are wondering what they'd be getting with a guy who hasn't played in more than two seasons and spent the offseason giving off more than a whiff of potential volatility. Aiyuk and his agent are going to have to work hard to make the case that he's ready to step in to help a team right now.

Quick straw poll time: Which name is coming up most often in MVP conversations with people around the league?

Graziano: The name I've heard the most lately is Joe Burrow, and I don't think a down game on Monday night necessarily changes that. He's playing at a ludicrously high level for a team that's in first place and doesn't really run the ball. People also have started bringing up Brock Purdy seriously. I think the tendency to view Purdy as strictly a scheme fit who's along for the ride with the 49ers' stars and coaches is fading, and he's seen as a bigger part of their success than he used to be. In essence, perception is catching up with reality.

Maybe it's the 49ers' much-publicized injury issues at wide receiver that have people appreciating Purdy's value more than they once did, but it seems like the tide has turned on how he's perceived. Draft status sticks with a guy throughout his career, right or wrong, and there has been a widespread hesitation to view Purdy as a top quarterback because he was the 262nd pick in 2022. He keeps proving that wrong, and if the 49ers keep winning and he stays healthy, he could end up winning this award.

Fowler: Burrow and Purdy are the clear leaders, and the debate between them is a toss-up, with Patrick Mahomes right behind them. I agree with you regarding draft status. Purdy's "Mr. Irrelevant" reputation and lack of size often hurt him in the quarterback pantheon, with many team evaluators viewing him as a fringe top-10 guy. That's clearly not the case anymore. He's putting together a season for the ages and has four games with at least three touchdown passes. His banner game against Brian Flores' defense Sunday night was a statement. Purdy is the best in the league at layering the ball and using short-area quickness to buy time to find the open receiver. And he's using his legs well, with 222 rushing yards on 41 carries.

While Purdy is probably the game's most consistent performer, Burrow is a little more prolific, which could give him the edge in this discussion. He's a legitimate threat to surpass 5,000 passing yards and 50 touchdowns despite a stagnant running game and minimal play-action/screen plays. It's all on Burrow. I would give him the slight edge right now, but it's very close ... which is why we get seven more games to find out.

Who's a sleeper, Dan? We mentioned Mahomes earlier. What about Jared Goff? He's always good yet always a bit underrated. This is five seasons of impressive play in Detroit.

Graziano: No doubt Goff is in this race at this point, but you're right. He's another player people are hesitant to credit for his team's success, and the overall excellence of the Lions' offense oddly works against him when it comes to rating him among the top QBs. It's unfair, but perception and narrative have an impact on MVP voting.

But I would be remiss if I didn't mention Jaxon Smith-Njigba in this discussion. No wide receiver has ever won the award, which makes sense, because wide receivers depend on quarterbacks for production. Ergo, how can a wide receiver possibly be more valuable? I've always thought that if a wide receiver were ever to win, it would have to be one who set a bunch of single-season records in a year when there was no clear QB winner. In Smith-Njigba's case, he's on pace for 2,052 receiving yards, which would set a record. He's far and away the most important and productive offensive player on the Seahawks. And he has produced with two different starting quarterbacks this season, Sam Darnold (seven games) and Drew Lock (three).

I doubt it can happen, but Smith-Njigba deserves at least a mention. His production is that exceptional.

Fowler: JSN is absolutely worthy, but the system appears set up for receivers and running backs to win Offensive Player of the Year, not MVP. If he can hit those marks while catalyzing a late-season charge for Seattle, perhaps he sways some voters. And he should.

It will be interesting to see whether Thursday night's Chiefs-Bills showdown alters the MVP conversation at all, given Mahomes' and Josh Allen's proximity to the award most years. Allen and Mahomes hold two of the past four MVP trophies. Allen's numbers aren't on par with the previous two seasons, but he's never too far away. And Mahomes' 13 touchdowns to zero interceptions over the past four games reminds of what he can do when healthy and protected up front. He has been sacked only 13 times.

What are you hearing on Puka Nacua? What is the most likely offseason outcome for him and the Rams?

Fowler: This is one of the most complicated free agency situations. When healthy, Nacua is the top free agent in the entire class, but his future in Los Angeles seems shaky. The Rams did not pursue an extension with Nacua over the summer despite his huge 129-catch season -- due in large part to his off-field troubles. The feeling was that the Rams could revisit his future down the line, giving him a chance to improve on and off the field. But now that his season is over because of MCL surgery, he will have missed 10 regular-season games, which could give the Rams pause on doing a megadeal.

The flip side: The franchise tag is projected to around $31 million for receivers in 2027, a relative bargain for a player of Nacua's caliber. Multiple execs and sources I checked with this week believe the Rams' best course is to tag him. Nacua has 70 catches for 715 receiving yards in seven games! Between the durability concerns and the three-game suspension for violating the personal conduct policy, I'm just not convinced that the Rams pay him what it would take to keep him on a long-term deal -- which is a lot.

Graziano: I agree. That they didn't seem to even do much work toward a possible extension this past offseason was a sign of their hesitancy, and the issues that have come up during the season surely haven't assuaged that. My sense all along has been that the most likely outcome is the Rams franchise-tagging him next spring and either keeping him for one more year or seeing what teams would be willing to trade for him.

I don't think it's out of the question that they do an extension, but it's tricky, because his performance on the field says he should be getting top-of-market, Jaxon Smith-Njigba-level money. But Nacua has missed a ton of games and is serving a personal conduct policy suspension while on injured reserve. His playing style clearly lends itself to potential injury, and investing long term in a player who's already showing signs of physical breakdown at age 25 is worrisome. Fundamentally, I wouldn't feel good about predicting that Nacua will be in a Rams uniform beyond 2027, and I wouldn't be completely stunned if he were elsewhere next season.

Fowler: The contract is a huge hurdle because of the sheer massive haul required for a player of Nacua's caliber. He's too accomplished to take a low-end deal. What's funny -- and one person in the league broached this with me -- is considering what it might look like if Los Angeles switched out Nacua for the other top free agent receiver, George Pickens. Pickens is a true outside receiver who's scheme transcendent, and Rams coach Sean McVay would be a good fit for him personality-wise. Pickens has been a good soldier in Dallas, and his market is big but not in that JSN range you mentioned earlier -- more in line with Baltimore's Zay Flowers and Atlanta's Drake London, at or around $35 million annually.

So, all of this with Nacua and the Rams seems, at best, uncertain, though his play style and on-field demeanor fits what the Rams represent, so maybe that's enough. It should be noted that Los Angeles likes to swoop in right before free agency with a satisfactory deal. The Rams did so with guard Kevin Dotson days before 2024 free agency began and with safety Quentin Lake in Week 18 of the 2025 season. That's a different caliber of player, but the point is a team's posture can always change.

Graziano: All fair points, but the flip side is that the Rams have also been a team that has moved on -- or at least considered moving on -- from players before it got too late. Todd Gurley, Brandin Cooks, Jalen Ramsey and Marcus Peters are among the examples. Even after Davante Adams had a big 2025 season, they mulled replacing him with A.J. Brown this past offseason. The Rams have a lot to figure out about their roster construction, regardless of how this season's all-in project turns out. Nacua could fit in the plans, but I'm not sure it's going to be as the highest-paid wide receiver in the league.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?

Graziano: I might try to get Saints running back Travis Etienne Jr. for the stretch run. The Saints want to lean on him in the run game, and I expect them to give him more work as he continues to work his way back from injury. Now, the Saints' run game is nothing to get excited about, but they have an excellent remaining schedule for fantasy running backs. They get the Bengals, Packers and Panthers the next three weeks. You might have to pivot in Week 15 against the Buccaneers, but if you can find another RB2 to help you survive that week, you can run Etienne out there against the Cardinals in Week 16 and the Falcons in Week 17 and feel pretty decent about it.

Fowler: Baltimore's Justice Hill is a sensible RB2 or flex play for a struggling roster. Derrick Henry appears to be approaching the inevitable wall that he has staved off for years, averaging a career-low 4.0 yards per carry. With quarterback Jacoby Brissett, the Ravens appear comfortable with a pass-happy offense. That's good for Hill, who is more adept at catching the ball out of the backfield. While Henry will continue to tote the rock, Hill has turned 69 snaps into 18 touches for 143 total yards and a touchdown since Week 10 (and that's not counting his 65-yard rushing score in Week 9).

description:
Green Bay Packers star defensive end Micah Parsons hasn’t played an NFL game since Dec. 14, 2025.

He talked on his podcast, “The Edge with Micah Parsons,” about his return from injury and how rehab felt.

text:
Green Bay Packers star defensive end Micah Parsons hasn’t played an NFL game since Dec. 14, 2025. It has been 345 days and counting since he last stepped onto an NFL Field.

Parsons is expected to make his 2026 debut in Week 12 against the Los Angeles Rams. The Packers are getting the Penn State product at just the right time. They’re in an absolute dogfight in the NFC North and are trying to make a playoff push. Parsons will bolster the Green Bay defense and put every quarterback on notice.

He talked on his podcast, “The Edge with Micah Parsons,” about his return from injury and how rehab felt.

MORE: Super Bowl champ says Bears-Lions clash could decide more than NFC North title

Micah Parsons shares thoughts on return from injury

Micah Parsons is itching to get back on the field. He was candid on his podcast about what he learned about himself during rehab:

“The one thing I learned and loved about myself the most is that I’m a better man not because of what happened to me is about because I’m a better man about how I reacted what happened to me. And I say that is like the injury didn’t make me want to be a better human.

“Like I just became a human because I said, ‘Hey, I’m going to attack this the same way that, you know, God would want me to.’ Like he’s putting this pressure on me. He’s throwing this at me. Do I know why? No. But I’m just going to attack this anyway. I needed this. No offense. I even said it to myself. It’s like no one could tell me anything. Like I felt invincible.”

Parsons talked about how great a season he was having in 2025 and all the emotions he felt when he got hurt. The 27-year-old had recorded 12.5 sacks and 41 tackles in 14 games before getting hurt.

The Packers were probably cautious about his return because he’s in the second year of his four-year, $186 million contract. They’ve invested a lot in him and want to make sure he’s 100 percent healthy before returning to the field.

He gave quarterbacks and offensive coordinators nightmares before his injury, and Parsons hopes to return to top form for Green Bay. How is the former Nittany Lion feeling before his first game of the season? He said “bro, I’m just so happy now.”

Parsons is expected to make his season debut in Week 12 at 8 p.m. ET Wednesday, Nov. 25, against the Rams. The game will be on Netflix.

Skyler Gill-Howard is out for the season Rookie Skyler Gill-Howard is done for the season.
On the more positive end, Campbell couldn’t give a firm answer on whether cornerback D.J.

The Lions lose Gill-Howard for the season, and that stings.
text:
Well, this is the stuff you hate talking about. Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell gave a round of injury updates on Tuesday ahead of Thursday’s Thanksgiving matchup with the Chicago Bears. Some of them were positive. Some of them were very negative.

Let’s start with the worst of them.

Skyler Gill-Howard is out for the season

Rookie Skyler Gill-Howard is done for the season. He injured his knee on the goal line on Sunday against Tampa Bay while playing offense, helping Jahmyr Gibbs get into the end zone. The injury is going to require surgery, and that ends his season.

We don’t know exactly what the injury is. All we know is it’s a knee injury that requires surgery.

It’s an absolute bummer. Gill-Howard was having a great rookie season, and it felt like he was growing every week. Now he’s going to be out for the foreseeable future, and Detroit loses a young player who was trending in the right direction.

On the more positive end, Campbell couldn’t give a firm answer on whether cornerback D.J. Reed will play against Chicago. He said Reed could be a game-time decision.

Here’s exactly what Campbell said:

“You know, he’s, he’s improving. I mean, I thought he ran around pretty pretty good yesterday, but it’s— I can’t give a definitive answer on that just yet. You know, probably come down to game time decision.”

Getting Reed back would be gigantic. This is a very good Bears offense, and you have to have your best guys out there. Before the injury, Reed was one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL over the last four or five games he played. Definitely keep an eye on that one.

Cade Mays should return before the end of the season

Next up is Cade Mays. The Lions believe they will get him back before the end of the season. He went on IR just before Detroit played Tampa Bay on Sunday, so if he does come back, it would be sometime in December.

Will he actually play when he returns? That I don’t know. Things are going well with Juice Scruggs right now, and you kind of feel like you should just keep it that way. We’ll see what happens.

Campbell explained why the team put Mays on IR:

“Just felt like It didn’t feel good the next 2 games for sure, possibly 3. So it just made sense, you know, because it’s, you know, these 2 games in a short period of time, you know, whatever that is, you get 2 of them knocked out and it buys you the roster spot. So just— but yeah, we feel like we’ll get him back.”

That’s the logic. With two games packed into a short window, the IR move costs Mays very little time while freeing up a roster spot.

Chuck Clark and D.J. Wonnum are up in the air

A couple of guys also popped up on Monday’s injury report for the Lions’ first practice of the week. Chuck Clark was one of them, and D.J. Wonnum was the other.

Campbell was asked if either would be able to play against the Bears.

“I can’t tell you. It’ll be game-time decisions on Chuck.”

Clark will be a game-time decision, and it sounds like Wonnum will be one, too.

This is what happens when you play three games in 12 days. You’re bound to have some guys getting roughed up. The good news is the Lions get a little mini-bye after this game on Thanksgiving. Before they get there, though, they have to make sure everybody is out there against Chicago.

You have to get Clark. You have to get Wonnum. Most importantly, you have to get Reed. When you’re facing an offense like this one, you need your best players on the field.

Game designations come out on Wednesday, and we’ll know more then. Until then, the hardest news of the day stands. The Lions lose Gill-Howard for the season, and that stings.

text:
Eagles cornerback Quinyon Mitchell was upgraded to a limited participant on the team’s injury report on Tuesday after beginning the week listed as a non-participant.

Because the Eagles’ held a walkthrough on Tuesday, their injury report was an estimation, just like Monday’s. But this is definitely good news for Mitchell. Earlier in the day, defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said he thought Mitchell would be “fine” for Thanksgiving against Dallas.

It’s also worth noting that Saquon Barkley (neck), Dallas Goedert (shin) and Tanner McKee (rib) were all upgraded to full participants after being listed as limited to start the week.

Barkley might not get back to 100% for the rest of the season, but he will be able to play on Thursday after leaving the Steelers game early with what looked like a stinger.

Here’s the Eagles’ full injury report from Tuesday:

DNP: OLB Arnold Ebiketie (oblique), CB Jonathan Jones (ankle)

Limited: CB Quinyon Mitchell (hamstring), LB Smael Mondon (ankle), RB Will Shipley (foot/illness)

NFL

Full: RB Saquon Barkley (neck/illness), DT Jalen Carter (quad), DB Michael Carter (abdomen), WR Britain Covey (knee), TE Dallas Goedert (shin), OLB Jonathan Greenard (ankle), QB Tanner McKee (rib), CB Kelee Ringo (neck), WR DeVonta Smith (hamstring)

In addition to Mitchell, linebacker Smael Mondon (ankle) was also upgraded from DNP to limited on Tuesday. That’s good news because he would be the Eagles’ top backup behind Jihaad Campbell and Jeremiah Trotter Jr., who are both starters with Zack Baun (back) on Injured Reserve.

With this quick turnaround, the Eagles are not planning on having a full practice at all this week. It’ll be all walkthroughs to prepare for this NFC East battle on Thursday afternoon.

text:
Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III, who has missed the last two games with a groin injury, returned to practice on Tuesday as his team gets ready for a Thanksgiving night matchup at the Buffalo Bills.

Head coach Andy Reid told reporters on Tuesday that Walker wasn't expected to do "a ton of work."

Walker was ultimately listed as a limited participant in practice.

Walker has been exceptional for the 8-2 Chiefs, totaling 1,044 yards from scrimmage and 11 touchdowns in eight games.

The reigning Super Bowl MVP arrived in town after the Chiefs signed the ex-Seattle Seahawk to a three-year, $43.1 million contract. He's been a driving force for the Chiefs' turnaround after Kansas City went 6-11 last season.

Unfortunately, Walker suffered the injury during his team's Thursday, Nov. 12 practice. Reid characterized the injury as a "sore groin."

"It's getting better," Reid told reporters last Wednesday. We just don't want to do something stupid. He's feeling better."

Rookie Emmett Johnson has taken his place over the last two weeks, which has featured the Chiefs outscoring the Atlanta Falcons (35-13) and Arizona Cardinals (34-7) by 49 points. During that stretch, Johnson has rushed for 206 yards and a touchdown while adding 108 receiving yards and two scores on 10 receptions.

Ultimately, the Chiefs got the best of both worlds. They enjoyed a pair of comfortable wins while Walker was able to rest and get right for the stretch run.

Walker missed the team's walkthrough on Monday, but his Tuesday practice participation, even in a limited capacity, is a good sign for his availability on Thursday.

It's a massive game for the Chiefs, who are (a) tied with the 8-2 Denver Broncos for the AFC West lead and (b) simultaneously trying to chase down the 9-1 Bills for the AFC's No. 1 spot.
